Definition

Oxygen therapy means the use of supplemental oxygen for medical treatment

Nenad Stojkovic, CC BY 2.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Oxygen storage

Oxygen can be stored as a compressed gas in a high pressure oxygen storage cylinders

Oxygen also stored as a liquid in dewar, cryogenic liquid cylinder

Pawar0365, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Oxygen concentrators are also available for long term home use

They work by concentrating the oxygen from the room air by selectively removing nitrogen using electricity

i_am_jim, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Oxygen delivery devices

Oxygen is commonly delivered to the patient through nasal cannula

Nasal cannula can provide oxygen at low flow rates from 1-6 liters per minute, and capable of delivering oxygen concentration of 24-40%

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Oxygen is commonly delivered to the patient through simple face mask

Simple face mask can provide oxygen at 5- 10 liters per minute, and capable of delivering oxygen concentration of 35-55%

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Oxygen also can be delivered through venturi mask

Venturi mask can accurately deliver a predetermined oxygen concentration of 24-50%

Open Critical Care & World Health Organization, CC BY 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Oxygen also can be delivered through a partial rebreather mask which based on a simple mask but with a reservoir bag

Partial rebreather mask can provide oxygen at 5- 15 liters per minute, and capable of delivering oxygen concentration of 40-70%

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Oxygen also can be delivered through a non rebreather mask (reservoir mask) which draws oxygen from attached reservoir bag with on way valves that direct exhaled air out of the mask

Partial rebreather mask can provide oxygen at > 10 liters per minute, and capable of delivering oxygen concentration of 60-80%

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Oxygen also can be delivered through the bag valve mask, endotracheal tube, laryngeal mask airway, it can be given through bypassing the airway in ECMO (extracorporeal membrane oxygenation) therapy

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Indications of oxygen therapy

Acute hypoxic conditions: acute MI, acute pulmonary edema, carbon monoxide poisoning, cardiac and respiratory arrest, major trauma, anaphylaxis, major bleeding, shock, active convulsions, hypothermia, metabolic acidosis ( bicarbonate < 18 mmol/l) and decompression sickness

Chronic hypoxic conditions (long-term oxygen therapy): COPD, cystic fibrosis, chronic bronchitis, emphysema and heart failure

It is also used in treatment of cluster headache and in induction of anesthesia

British medical journal recommends that oxygen therapy is stopped for saturations > 96%; and it should not be started for saturations > 90% (there is association between excessive oxygenation and mortality)

Exceptions for this rule is carbon monoxide poisoning, cluster headaches, sickle cell crisis and pneumothorax

In cases of carbon monoxide toxicity or cardiac arrest, saturations should be as high as possible

Oxygen therapy monitoring

Pulse oximetry or ABG analysis is what is used for monitory of oxygen therapy

Oxygen should be titrated to a target level based on pulse oximetry of 94-96% in most patients or 88-92% in patients with COPD to avoid CO2 retention

Rcp.basheer, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Important notes

Hypoxia means low oxygen level at the tissues while hypoxemia means low oxygen level in the arterial blood

Dyspnea does not necessarily indicate hypoxemia. Severe hypoxemia can be present without dyspnea and vice versa

Oxygen therapy adverse effects

Oxygen should not be used routinely unless there is evidence of hypoxia because when used in excessively high concentrations, it can result in oxygen toxicity (lung damage, CNS damage and eyes damage) leading to respiratory failure and death

Oxygen can also dry out the airways if used without humidification leading to Irritation of nose, pharynx and trachea => mucus hypersecretion

In infants with respiratory failure, administration of high levels of oxygen may promote overgrowth of new blood vessels in the retina of the eye leading to blindness; this condition is known as retinopathy of prematurity

Oxygen therapy may also lead to CO2 retention; in those at risk (COPD patients), saturations of 88-92% are preferred

CO2 retention

In patients with COPD who receive supplementary O2, CO2 retention can occur through 2 mechanisms:

Increase O2 saturation of blood reduces deoxygenated Hb which carries CO2 in blood (in the forms of bicarbonate) => higher CO2 levels => more retention

In patients with COPD, hypoxia is the main drive of respiration, so If 100% O2 was administered, hypoxia is corrected and the hypoxic drive is lost leading to CO2 retention

Co2 retention can lead to headache, drowsiness (narcosis) or death

in people with COPD, CO2 toxicity can be prevented by maintaining oxygen saturation between 88-92%

Hazards and risks

Oxygen itself is not flammable but the addition of concentrated oxygen to a fire greatly increases its intensity; and concentrated oxygen can aid the combustion of material that are relatively inert under normal conditions
